newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel says Bundesbank gold revaluation necessary.
newsitem.headline: Waigel says Bundesbank gold revaluation necessary.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Thursday his intention to revalue the Bundesbank's gold reserves remained necessary despite the central bank's strong objection to the plan.

Waigel told journalists that "not a single mark from a revaluation of the reserve stock would be funneled" into Bonn's budget, which critics have said would help ready Germany for entry into Europe's currency union.

"It will not go into the budget but it will go step by step into the Inherited Debt Redemption Fund and the Bundesbank thinks this practice from 1999 on is appropriate," Waigel said of the funds to be received from revaluing gold and foreign exchange reserves nearer to market prices.
Under guidelines for European monetary union, national central bank gold reserves need to be revalued in preparation for the new European Central Bank.
Waigel noted, "What is right in 1999 cannot be wrong in 1997 and 1998."

The Bundesbank has said Waigel's plan to revalue German gold reserves and transfer part of the gains to Bonn as early as 1997 ran the risk of damaging confidence in the stability of the new currency, to be called the euro.

EU nations that want to join the first wave of European monetary union must, among other conditions specified in the Maastricht Treaty, have a 1997 budget deficit of no more than three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) and a debt of no more than 60 percent of GDP.
Waigel said there was no doubt about Germany qualifying for currency union. "Germany can meet the EMU criteria even without the reserve revaluation," he said.

Waigel reaffirmed his support for Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer, saying the central bank chief has the full confidence of the German government and said he had no knowledge of any resignation threat by Tietmeyer.
